Q: My quantregForest model returns inconsistent predictions A:

The program trains a Quantile Regression Forest 100 times, makes predictions each time, removes missing predictions, and prints the number of valid predictions.

print() displays the result on the screen.

So:

print(length(pred[!is.na(pred)]))

prints the number of non-missing predictions after every iteration.

In simple words:

The program trains a Quantile Regression Forest 100 times, using 20 trees each time, predicts values for d, and prints the number of valid predictions obtained in each run.

Q: I can't remove python pip A:

If you are a Windows user, make sure you run 'python -m pip uninstall pip' in administrator mode.

Q: How can i make Syntax highlighting for a custom extension? A:

If you want to design your own extension for Visual Studio, such as designing your own syntax highlighter, you must install Visual Studio SDK first, which enables you to design the extension and create VSIX package to install it.

To install Visual Studio SDK should be easy. Just go to your Visual Studio Installer (starting from VS2017, I guess, all versions of VS leverage this same stand-alone installer), click Modify on your VS version, scroll down until you see the section "Other Toolsets". In that section you should see an item labelled as "Visual Studio extension development", select its checkbox before clicking the Modify button. That should install the Visual Studio SDK for you, plus some supplementary packages such as the related templates / assemblies. After doing so, restart your Visual Studio and you will be able to see a new template for creating extension when you want to create a new project.

But the rest is hard work, of course. You need to learn how to write extensions for Visual Studio. Here's its on-line document:

Visual Studio Extensibility - Visual Studio (Windows) | Microsoft Learn

Q: How do I extract a valid command line(s) from a VS Code launch.json file? A:

You can use program jq to extract data from JSON file and reformat them

It gets all elements in list "configurations", joins elements in args to one string using space as separator,

  • next it creates list only with name and args (if there can be other values) and again it joins them to one string with space.
jq '.configurations[] | .args |= join(" ") | [.name, .args] | join(" ")' launch.json
  • or it formats string directly using values name, args
jq '.configurations[] | .args |= join(" ") | "\(.name) \(.args)"' launch.json

(char | means piping like in bash)

Result:

"myprog foo1 bar1 foo2 bar2 etc andsoon"
"other --text long text with spaces --hello world"

but (at this moment) it doesn't add quotation marks for arguments which have spaces.

Q: How do I atomically create a locked file in Linux? A:

The best solution is probably to save files being downloaded separately. Let's suppose we are downloading into cache key foo, a trivial

if open("foo.cache", O_RDONLY):
  return fd, file is here and fully downloaded

if open("foo.tmp", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL):
  if open("foo.cache", O_RDONLY):
    unlink(foo.tmp)
    return fd for foo.cache
  download()
  rename("foo.tmp", "foo.cache")
  return fd, file is here and fully downloaded

/* there's another process currently downloading into foo */
sleep and retry

This is simple and will solve the scenario in most cases, but the polling is not particularly elegant (although it will hardly matter for performance)

We can make it wait on a lock by doing:

if open("foo.cache", O_RDONLY):
  return fd, file is here and fully downloaded

if open("foo.tmp", O_WRONLY | O_CREAT | O_EXCL):
  lock(foo.tmp)
  if open("foo.cache", O_RDONLY):
    unlink(foo.tmp)
    close(fd.tmp)
    return fd for foo.cache
  download()
  rename("foo.tmp", "foo.cache")
  unlock()
  return fd, file is here and fully downloaded

/* there's another process currently downloading into foo */

while open("foo.tmp", O_RDONLY):
  lock(foo.tmp)
  if open("foo.cache", O_RDONLY):
    close(fd.tmp)
    return fd for foo.cache

  /* we won a race on open+lock that we wanted to lose */
  close(fd.tmp) /* implicitly unlocks */
  sleep /* yield so hopefully it is now won by the creating process */

if not open("foo.cache", O_RDONLY):
  abort() /* should not happen */

return fd for foo.cache

albeit there is still a case where it goes to sleep to relinquish a lock it did not expect to obtain

Using a separate filename (or downloading them into a different folder in the same filesystem) ensures that the .cache files are always consistent, even in the case of unexpected conditions (downloading program dying/being killed mid-operation, filesystem getting full, hardware crash¹... ).

However, if the downloading process fails, other clients would indefinitely block. You may want to include a periodic search for old .tmp files and delete them as stale.²

¹ you probably want to finish download() with a fdatasync() for this scenario

² you could verify stat("foo.tmp").inode == fstat(fd's "foo.tmp").inode before rename if you want to ensure you are not renaming a new .tmp that replaced your own

Q: Why specify the type again outside the class for initialization if declared in class already? A:

Why to specify the type again outside the class for initialization if declared in class already?

Because the one inside the class is only a "declaration" while the one outside the class is a "definition" and we need to specify the type when declaring/defining a variable.

then i can simply do 'i = 1;' at anywhere to define and initialize it.

No, declaration, definition and initialization are all different things in C++. Note that i = 1; is assignment while int i = 1; is definition which also includes initialization to 1. Also, int i; is also a definition. You may initialize a variable while defining it but that does not mean you don't need to specify the type. A type is required as per the rules of standard C++.

For example, we can have the following code from static documentation:

The declaration inside the class body is not a definition and may declare the member to be of incomplete type (other than void), including the type in which the member is declared:

struct S
{
   
   static S s;     // declaration, incomplete type (inside its own definition)
};
